title: An Experimental Protocol for Assessing the Performance of New Ultrasound Probes Based on CMUT Technology in Application to Brain Imaging
protocol: Preliminary design of the experimental setup.
Design an agar phantom for calibration procedures.
Prepare ex vivo bovine brain.
Acquire MR images of the brain.
Define qualitative poses for US image acquisition.
Set up experimental equipment and integrate instruments.
Calibrate the US probe with passive markers for navigation.
Acquire US images of the bovine brain in predefined poses.
Acquire US images in "freehand mode".
Post-process and visualize combined MR/US image dataset.
Prepare a polystyrene head mannequin by cutting out a shape similar to that of the bovine brain using a knife.
Insert 6 patterns of 3 Flint glass spheres (3 mm diameter) into the polystyrene brain, arranged at the vertices of an equilateral triangle with side of approximately 15 mm.
Connect the motion tracking system to the notebook via USB.
Open the tracking tool, start motion tracking and check that when touching the glass spheres in the polystyrene brain, the pointer tool remains within the tracking field of view.
In a beaker, dilute 100 g of glycerine and 30 g of agar in 870 g of distilled water.
Stir the mixture while increasing its temperature up to 90 °C for 10-15 min.
Pour the mixture to fill a 13x10x10 cm food container.
Keep the filled container in the refrigerator for at least one day.
Remove the agar phantom from the refrigerator.
Color 6 glass spheres with a yellow enamel.
Insert 2 patterns of 3 glass spheres each into the agar phantom, not farther than 1 mm from the surface.
Immerse the agar phantom in a solution of water and benzalkonium chloride for preservation.
Store the immersed agar phantom in a sealed plastic food container in the refrigerator.
Remove the brain from ice and place it in an aspirating hood.
Isolate the cerebral hemispheres by separating cerebellum, mesencephalon, pons, and brainstem with a surgical blade.
Cut through the structures on the ventral surface of the brain.
Use a polystyrene mannequin as a reference for positioning.
Implant 6 triangular patterns of 3 spheres each in the cortex of frontal, temporal, and occipital lobes.
Ensure predefined conditions (i.e., distances from the surface and among spheres) are met.
Mark the positions of all the spheres on brain surface with green tissue marking dye for histology.
Immerse the brain in 10% buffered formalin solution.
Use a plastic container for anatomical parts.
Leave the brain in the container with formalin for at least 3 weeks until fixation process is complete.
Extract the bovine brain from the formalin solution.
Wash the brain in water overnight.
Place the washed brain in a clean plastic container.
Seal the container securely.
Position the sealed container inside the MR head coil.
Insert the MR head coil containing the brain into the MR scanner.
Perform MR scans using a 3 T MR scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil.
Acquire three sets of images using T1 sequence.
Acquire three sets of images using T2 sequence.
Acquire three sets of images using CISS sequence.
Save the acquired MR images in DICOM format.
Immerse the brain in 10% buffered formalin after scanning.
Transfer the MR images from the scanner to a processing workstation.
Open the MR images in DICOM format with Paraview software tool.
Have an expert visualize the images as slices and 3D volume.
Inspect each MR image in the dataset to assess anatomical structures and tissues.
Select 3D spatial subregions containing best recognizable visual features.
Define cutting planes of maximal visibility for selected regions.
Identify 12 predefined poses for US image acquisition.
For each virtual pose, create a 3D Cone as a visual landmark using "Sources > Cone".
Adapt cone height to 40 mm and radius to 2 mm.
Manually position the cone in the 3D visual field.
Save MR image, 3D regions, planes, and landmarks as a Paraview state file.
Position a 50x50x30 cm plastic tank on a table.
Fill the tank with degassed water up to a height of 15 cm.
Position the motion tracking system so that the water tank is visible from above and entirely within its field of view.
Connect the motion tracker to the notebook via USB.
Perform the pivoting procedure to calibrate the pointer using the tracking tool of the motion tracking system.
Position the ULA-OP system on the table.
Connect the ULA-OP system to the notebook via USB, ensuring the computer screen is clearly visible to the US probe operator.
Position the workstation on the table and ensure its screen is clearly visible to the operator.
Extract the brain from formalin solution.
Wash the brain in water.
Immobilize the brain onto a plate of synthetic resin using segments of sewing thread and adhesive stripes.
Immerse the plate with the brain into the tank.
Verify that the entire working space around the brain fits within the field of view of the motion tracker, using the pointer and software tracking tool.
Connect the US probe to the ULA-OP system.
Configure the ULA-OP system through its configuration files and software interface from the computer.
Define a duplex-mode consisting of two interleaved B-modes employing two different operating frequencies (7 MHz and 9 MHz).
Set a 1-cycle bipolar burst for each mode.
Set the transmission focus at 25 mm depth.
Configure dynamic focusing in reception with F#=2 sinc apodization function.
Configure the system to record beamformed and I/Q demodulated data.
Perform acquisition tests to ensure full operativity.
Click on the "Freeze" toggle button in the ULA-OP software to freeze the system.
Enable autosave mode by clicking on the three floppy disks toggle button.
Write the filename in the popup window at the end of the acquisition and click "Save".
Find a suitable position for the clamp on the US probe handle.
Clamp the passive reflective markers onto the US probe handle.
Perform acquisition tests to ensure that the clamp is stable, the markers are visible by the motion tracking system while the US probe is held in expected working postures.
Position the agar phantom in full immersion inside the water tank.
Start the logging application that records position data.
Collect the positions of each of the 6 glass spheres in the agar phantom with the pointer tool.
Track the motion of the pointer tool while collecting sphere positions.
Acquire one US image per each pattern of 3 spheres in the agar phantom.
Position the US probe via the mechanical arm using the pre-visualization function of the ULA-OP system.
Ensure a complete pattern of three spheres is within the field of view for imaging.
Acquire and save the corresponding US image.
Transfer all US images in ULA-OP format to the workstation.
Together with motion tracker log-files, transfer files to the workstation.
Open each US image in the visualization software.
Manually mark the position of the 3 glass spheres in each image.
Transcribe the 3D positions into a .csv file.
Compute the US-to-marker rigid transformation between the two reference frames.
Position the brain in full immersion inside the water tank.
Start the logging application and collect the positions of each of the 18 glass spheres with the pointer tool.
Transfer the motion tracker log files onto the workstation.
Open each MR image of the brain in the visualization software.
Manually mark the position of each of the 18 glass spheres.
Save the corresponding 3D coordinates as .csv files.
Compute the motion tracker-to-MR rigid transformation between the two reference frames.
Acquire the positions of the glass spheres implanted in the bovine brain for calibration using the pointer tool tip, one by one.
Use the acquired positions to compute the transformation from the motion tracking system space to the MR image space.
Clamp the markers onto the US probe and execute the calibration procedure.
Position the brain and execute the calibration procedure.
Collect the two rigid transformation parameters (US-to-marker and motion tracker-to-MR) computed in previous steps.
Transfer these files into the folder of the real-time visualization procedure implemented in Python.
Start the real-time visualization procedure using the visualization software.
Verify that the actual position of the US probe is displayed correctly.
Start the logging application for recording the position of the probe.
Manually match each qualitatively predefined position with the US probe as displayed in the visualization software.
Acquire the corresponding image with the ULA-OP system.
Stop the two applications.
Transfer all US images in ULA-OP format and motion tracker log files to the workstation.
Clamp markers onto the US probe and execute calibration procedure.
Position the brain and execute calibration procedure.
Manually position the US probe at the intended initial pose.
Start acquisition of each US image sequence with the ULA-OP system.
Apply slow, freehand motion to the US probe towards the intended final pose.
Stop acquisition of US images with the ULA-OP system.
Transfer all US images in ULA-OP format and motion tracker log files to workstation.
Load sequence of US images in ULA-OP format.
Match sequence of US images with motion tracker log files.
Extract sequence of timed positions from log files within start-to-end acquisition interval.
Compute exact timing of each US image in the sequence using parameters recorded by ULA-OP system.
Compute the position associated with each US image by interpolating between the two closest timed positions recorded by the motion tracking system.
Use linear interpolation between translation vectors for interpolation.
Express rotations as quaternions and use spherical linear interpolation (SLERP).
Define the 3D US image frame using the median US image in the sequence as a reference.
Apply logarithmic compression to each plane in the US image.
Normalize the compressed image to its maximum value.
Apply a threshold of typically -60 dB to each plane.
Compute and apply a relative spatial transform with respect to the reference frame for each other US image in the sequence.
Save the Cartesian 3D array of voxels as a .vtk file.
Record interval timestamps that correspond to acquisition timing.
Load the US image in the ULA-OP format.
Apply logarithmic compression, normalize the image to its maximum value, and apply a threshold of typically -60 dB to each plane.
Apply a linear interpolation routine to the structure of spatially-located planes for 3D US images.
Save the image plane or Cartesian 3D array of voxels as a .vtk file, recording interval timestamps that correspond to acquisition timing.
Load the US image in .vtk format.
Match the timing of the US image with motion tracker log files.
Extract a sequence of timed positions from the log files included in the temporal interval going from the start to the end of the acquisition process, as recorded in the .vtk image.
Compute an average position for the US image using linear averaging for translation vectors and applying the algorithm described for rotations expressed as quaternions.
Load the US-to-marker transformation corresponding to the specific US image.
Load the motion tracker-to-MR transformation corresponding to the specific US image and the MR image of choice.
Compute the US-to-MR rigid registration transformation using the average position and the loaded transformations.
Save the US-to-MR rigid registration transformation in different formats, including translation and Euler angles.
Start the visualization software and load the MR image of choice.
Load all relevant US images.
For each US image, create a Paraview Transform.
Apply the computed US-to-MR registration transformation to the image data.
Compute the desired transformation RTS>MRI from the 3D positions of spheres measured in both the motion tracking system frame and the target MR image using the algorithm described.
Compute the transformation RM>TS directly from the US image acquisition procedure as specified.
Calculate RUS>MRI by multiplying RTS>MRI with RM>TS.
Calculate tUS>MRI using the formula: tUS>MRI = RTS>MRI * (RM>TS * tUS>M + tM>TS) + tTS>MRI.
